title: Reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation

guidelineVersions: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway, Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Instability (2015)

brief.scenario: A 25-year-old man presents after a fall onto an outstretched arm while playing football. His right shoulder is visibly deformed and painful, and radiographs demonstrate an anterior glenohumeral dislocation without an apparent associated fracture. He is alert and haemodynamically stable. A shoulder model is provided.
brief.task: You are the core surgical trainee. Assess the patient and the need for reduction, obtain consent, demonstrate a controlled reduction approach on the model, and describe post-reduction assessment and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A safe reduction begins and ends with documented neurovascular status and radiographic assessment.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Using force without analgesia, fracture review or pre/post-reduction axillary nerve and vascular examination.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Before reduction I will check the X-ray, document axillary nerve sensation and distal vascular status, and agree analgesia and supervision.

flow: Confirm diagnosis, mechanism and associated injury; inspect pre-reduction radiographs.
Document axillary nerve, other peripheral nerve function and distal perfusion before moving the joint.
Explain procedure, obtain consent, ensure suitable analgesia or sedation resources and trained assistance.
Use a gentle locally approved reduction technique on the model; abandon excessive force or repeated failed attempts.
Repeat neurovascular examination, obtain post-reduction imaging, immobilise appropriately and arrange follow-up.

grid.label: Identity and injury history
grid.fail: Does not check side or mechanism
grid.borderline: Confirms side but not mechanism or previous instability
grid.pass: Confirms injury, affected side and mechanism
grid.high: Screens high-energy injury and prior instability

grid.label: Pre-reduction imaging
grid.borderline: Looks at imaging but does not check for fracture or a second view
grid.pass: Reviews appropriate radiographs before routine reduction
grid.high: Recognises exceptions requiring emergency senior decision

grid.label: Pre-reduction neurovascular exam
grid.borderline: Checks pulses or axillary nerve, not both, or does not document
grid.pass: Documents lateral-deltoid sensation and distal circulation/motor function
grid.high: Identifies neurovascular deficit and escalates before manipulation

grid.label: Analgesia/consent
grid.fail: Attempts without consent or pain control
grid.borderline: Gives analgesia but incomplete risk explanation or consent
grid.pass: Explains risks and obtains consent with analgesia plan
grid.high: Checks sedation resources, monitoring and trained staff if required

grid.label: Gentle technique
grid.borderline: Controlled technique but poor positioning or explanation
grid.pass: Demonstrates controlled non-forceful reduction on model
grid.high: Stops early when resistance suggests complication

grid.label: Recognition of difficulty
grid.borderline: Makes one further unassisted attempt before seeking help
grid.pass: Stops failed attempts and seeks senior/orthopaedic help
grid.high: Anticipates fracture, soft-tissue block or neurovascular compromise

grid.label: Post-reduction neurovascular exam
grid.borderline: Repeats only part of the examination or does not document it
grid.pass: Repeats and records nerve and pulse examination

grid.label: Confirmation/immobilisation
grid.borderline: Requests one post-reduction view only, or no immobilisation
grid.pass: Obtains post-reduction radiographs and supports arm
grid.high: Checks alignment, associated fractures and neurovascular changes

grid.label: Follow-up and counselling
grid.borderline: Gives sling advice but no safety-net or follow-up
grid.pass: Explains immobilisation, return precautions and follow-up
grid.high: Discusses recurrence and rehabilitation appropriate to age/activity

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I can see the shoulder is out. I will pull it back in now.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: It hurts badly. Can I have something for pain?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It will only take a second.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I do not review the X-ray or check pulses and axillary nerve sensation.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: There is resistance to the first reduction attempt.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I pull harder and rotate the arm forcefully until it moves.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Good. Put it in a sling and go home.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am the core surgical trainee. Can I confirm your name and which shoulder you injured?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: My right. I fell playing football.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you injured this shoulder before or noticed tingling or weakness in the arm?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No previous dislocation, and no tingling.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I check the shoulder contour and review the pre-reduction X-rays for fracture and direction of dislocation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The film shows an anterior dislocation without visible fracture.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I assess the radial pulse, hand perfusion, finger and wrist movements and sensation over the lateral deltoid, documenting the findings before reduction.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Pulse, hand movement and lateral deltoid sensation are intact.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The joint needs reducing. I will explain the benefits and risks including pain, fracture and nerve or vessel injury, and obtain consent. You will receive appropriate analgesia; sedation, if required, needs monitoring and competent staff.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: We will manage the pain and use gentle controlled movements rather than forcing the shoulder. Please tell me if you feel severe pain or tingling.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: On the model, I position and support the arm and demonstrate a locally approved gentle reduction method.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The first gentle attempt is unsuccessful; there is firm resistance.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I stop; I will not apply increasing force or make repeated attempts. I recheck symptoms and seek senior or orthopaedic help.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A supervised reduction is now successful.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I immediately reassess and document axillary nerve sensation, hand motor function, capillary refill and pulses.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I request post-reduction radiographs, provide a sling as appropriate and arrange follow-up and rehabilitation advice.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes, recurrence is possible, particularly in younger active patients. Follow-up will discuss stability, rehabilitation and whether specialist review is needed. Return urgently for new numbness, weakness, severe pain or a cold hand.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. I will treat your pain, assess your arm carefully, and explain each step before we attempt reduction. Which shoulder was injured and how?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: The right. I fell while playing football and it immediately looked wrong.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Was this a direct blow or a fall onto the hand? Any previous episode, neck injury, tingling or hand weakness?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I fell onto the hand. No previous episode and no tingling.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I confirm the deformity and inspect the radiographs for dislocation direction and associated greater tuberosity or neck fracture before considering routine reduction.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Anterior dislocation, with no visible fracture.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I document a precise baseline: axillary nerve sensation over the regimental-badge area, relevant motor function where pain permits, distal pulses, colour, capillary refill and other peripheral nerve function.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I explain that gentle reduction usually relieves pain, but there is a risk of further injury. I obtain consent and choose analgesia; any procedural sedation would require a separate monitored, staffed pathway.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I am frightened you will pull hard.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will not force it. We will position you comfortably, relax the muscles and use a controlled technique, with a colleague assisting as appropriate.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: On the model I demonstrate a low-force technique and observe the patient throughout for pain or neurovascular change.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The humeral head does not reduce with the first gentle manoeuvre.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I stop here. Increasing force risks humeral or glenoid injury; I reassess pain, neurovascular status and imaging and request senior orthopaedic assistance before any further attempt.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Following specialist input, the shoulder reduces.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I repeat the same documented neurovascular examination immediately so we can identify a new deficit rather than merely describe the hand as “fine.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I request post-reduction AP and appropriate orthogonal imaging to confirm alignment and assess associated injury, support the arm, and give written safety advice and follow-up arrangements.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I want to play football again. Will it dislocate again?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Young active people have a meaningful recurrence risk. You should receive orthopaedic or shoulder-service follow-up and rehabilitation advice before return to sport. Urgent return is needed for recurrent deformity, tingling, weakness, colour change or uncontrolled pain.

failures.consequence: Missed pre-existing or worsened nerve or vascular injury.

failures.move: Failure to reassess new post-reduction paraesthesia.

recovery.when: If you have not documented axillary nerve sensation and pulses
recovery.line: I have not documented axillary nerve sensation and pulses; I will stop and examine before any reduction.

recovery.when: If it is not reducing with a gentle technique
recovery.line: It is not reducing with a gentle technique; I will stop and get senior orthopaedic help rather than use more force.

knowledge.fact: Pre-reduction evaluation includes identification of associated injuries.
Reduction should be performed promptly with adequate pain control and trained personnel.
Repeat neurovascular assessment is required after reduction.
Post-reduction imaging assesses congruity and associated fracture.
Young active patients carry greater risk of recurrent anterior instability.
Follow-up and rehabilitation are components of the full care pathway.

recall.think: Imaging and baseline nerve/vessel findings before any reduction.
recall.say: Explain analgesia, the gentle plan, injury risks and consent.
do: Controlled model reduction; stop when resistance persists.

numbers.meaning: greater tuberosity fracture in about 16% of anterior dislocations
almost 90% of recurrences occur within 2 years. No fixed force or number of attempts is a safe target.

recall.trap: Calling a visibly reduced shoulder safe without reassessment.
recall.finish: Repeat neurovascular checks, confirm on X-ray, support and refer.

sources.name: Brownson P et al. BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathways: Traumatic anterior shoulder instability. Shoulder & Elbow 2015;7(3):214–226

partner.opening: Assess the patient and the need for reduction, obtain consent, demonstrate a controlled reduction approach on the model, and describe post-reduction assessment and management.
partner.actorBrief: Patient opening: “My shoulder is out and the pain is awful.” If asked, he reports no numbness or hand weakness.

reveals.finding: Examiner provides normal distal pulses and intact lateral-deltoid sensation before reduction if examined.
X-ray shows uncomplicated anterior dislocation without visible fracture.

push.question: After successful assisted reduction, the patient asks whether the shoulder can come out again.

curveballs.prompt: Curveball after an initial model attempt: examiner says the joint is not reducing with gentle technique.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Candidate must stop rather than force it.
